wsl-claude: agreed on the principle: nothing face- or grant-specific goes into the core. But checked against the tree, the passthrough needs THREE small GENERIC core pieces besides the api spec, and I'd rather name them now than have them look like scope creep later:
1) STARTING grantFace. Today the node starts servers only as faceServer ('js/server.js --app <name>', appServers.js startAll). grantFace isn't a faceServer, so the node needs 'start this app's own server entry, keep it running' from its manifest.
2) THE DOOR ADDRESS. Server jobs are spawned without SPIRIT_CALLBACK_URL (startServerJob; only 'process' jobs get it, jobs.js:210), so grantFace can't reach the loopback interface you ruled it uses.
3) ASK FROM A PROCESS. The node's lowest-layer client (spirit.core ask) is page-relative, so it needs to aim at that address outside a browser.
All three know nothing about faces or grants; any server app would need them. With those named, yes: core = generic puppets + generic process + the api passthrough, and nothing else.

Almost. Checked against the tree, besides the passthrough/api spec the core needs two more generic changes. Neither knows about faces or grants:
1) A SERVER PROCESS RUNS ITS APP'S OWN CODE. Today the process the node starts for a serving app runs faceServer.js, which only hands out files (appServer.js:1039, now faceServer.js). grantFace has logic, so the node must start the app's own module instead, the way it already starts process jobs from process/js.
2) THE SPIRIT OBJECT WORKS OUTSIDE A PAGE. spirit.core.ask calls fetch('/api/spirit') (kernel.js:647), which only works in a browser. A server process needs the same call aimed at its node's door (the address the node hands a process job, SPIRIT_CALLBACK_URL).
Everything else is app scope: grantFace, its client page, the face's contact sync by owner.command, and the face carrying 'contact' (face-install, done).
So: the passthrough/api spec, plus these two floors. If you count them as part of 'generic passthrough', then yes, agreed.

agreed. 1) the process spec needs updating, including implementations of those updates. grantFace is a faceless spirit app, responding to HTTP equivalent requests. 2) the proccess spec DOES have a way of finding the owner-nodes api port, that's how the console windows in the jobs app get updated after all, there is a process interface in the node. that's where my requirement came from: the app-Servers must runn in the process-subsystem. look at the code for our image tagging systems to see how processes access node interfaces.

wsl-claude: you're right, and I overstated 2) and 3). Checked in imageCaptionClaude: a process requires kernel.js and gets spirit.core (fs, annotations, jobs.log), and jobs.report posts to SPIRIT_CALLBACK_URL, the node's own door. That's the process interface, and a verb call to the node is the same post.
So the real gap is one line, not three: the NEW 'server' job kind (startServerJob, built tonight for the app servers) spawns without SPIRIT_JOB_ID and SPIRIT_CALLBACK_URL, and only the old 'process' kind passes them (jobs.js:205-210). It left the process subsystem's contract on the way in. Fix: server jobs get the same two variables, and are then ordinary processes that happen to stay up. That's exactly your 'app servers must run in the process subsystem'.
Test: a server job can call jobs.log and a node verb through the callback, the same way imageCaption does.
taking team/chat (process spec update; processes reach the node like the image jobs)

Agreed, and you're right that the process interface exists. Checked in the image jobs: imageCaptionClaude requires the kernel and uses spirit.core.fs.* and spirit.core.jobs.* directly. jobs.* reaches the node through SPIRIT_CALLBACK_URL, the door address the node hands every process job (jobs.js:206, kernel.js:568). So the floor under grantFace is just finishing that interface:
1) A 'server' job gets the same two variables as a process job. Today startServerJob passes neither; I built it that way this afternoon.
2) spirit.core.ask uses SPIRIT_CALLBACK_URL when there's no page, so a process can call any verb a page can, owner.command included.
3) A serving app's own module runs as that server job, a faceless spirit app answering HTTP-equivalent requests, the way image jobs run from process/js.
ONE THING I FOUND: there's no written process spec. The code is the spec (jobs.js startProcessJob, kernel.js:549-603). So 'update the spec' means WRITING it: design/node/PROCESSES.md, covering what exists plus these three.
Go! = write PROCESSES.md, then implement 1-3.
